newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa mulls sending troops to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa mulls sending troops to Zaire.

text.p: South Africa on Wednesday suspended arms sales to Rwanda and indicated it would contribute troops to an international force for Zaire if asked to do so by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.
"We have taken a decision to temporarily suspend all arms sales to Rwanda," Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told a news conference.
He said the bulk of a 86.8 million rand ($18.5 million) arms contract with Rwanda, agreed at the end of September, comprised armoured personnel carriers.

The decision to suspend the contract followed reports that Rwandan forces were taking part in fighting in eastern Zaire between the region's rival Tutsi and Hutu tribes. The fighting has sparked a flood of tens of thousands of refugees out of the area.
Referring to a regional summit on the crisis in Nairobi on Tuesday, Pahad said "the most important decision was the call to set up safe corridors and therefore the need to deploy a neutral force".
Pahad said the U.N. Security Council was expected to meet this week to discuss the creation of an international force that would allow humanitarian aid to get to the refugees.
Asked if South Africa, which has one of the continent's most powerful armies, would contribute to such a force, Pahad said:

"In the context of the decision that the Security Council takes, we will be in constant consultation with the defence force -- which has already started -- our intelligence services and other relevant structures to see how South Africa can respond.

"We are conscious that we are an important country in the African continent and we have a responsibility for the continent and it's in our broader interest to contribute as much as we can to find a lasting solution."

During the apartheid era the South African armed forces staged raids into several neighbouring countries, fighting a 15-year conflict in Angola against black liberation guerrillas and Cuban conventional forces.
But they have little experience in international peacekeeping operations.

"If the situation deteriorates further and there is an explosion as predicted it will affect all of us in the African continent and we will have serious consequences," Pahad said, referring to the possibility of the conflict splitting Zaire into separate entities.

He said former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere would arrive in South Africa on Saturday "to discuss the developing situation and what response the international community and South Africa can give".
Pahad said France had circulated a proposal for equal numbers of U.S., European Union and African troops to take part in an international force for eastern Zaire.
